Archery completely replaces vanilla Aiming for bows. None of a bow's four AimingPerk fields apply at all; hit chance, critical chance and range are folded onto the bow itself and scaled by your Archery level instead.

Archery XP comes from an arrow actually landing on a zombie - not from the hit-chance roll - plus a small amount every time you nock.

One vanilla effect does survive: a rifle-trained character still holds a bow very slightly steadier, because recoil, sway and sight range are read off the character rather than off the weapon, and are not reachable from Lua. That is accepted, not a bug.

Five Archery skill books raise how fast you learn. See the Skill books & Magazines page.

Every arrow in this mod follows the same shape: turn wood into a plain shaft, fletch the shaft, then haft a head onto it. The sealed packs shortcut part of that - a Carbon Arrow Shaft arrives already fletched, and the two manufactured heads cannot be made at all, only found.

Fletching XP scales with how far along the chain you are, so finishing an arrow is worth far more than carving the shaft it started as.

Broken arrows repair back into whole ones from their right-click Repair option - no recipe and no skill gate, though each attempt can still fail.

For the material roster - which head needs which skill, and what each sealed pack contains - see the Arrowheads & Shafts page. For how the faster recipe tiers unlock, see the Skill books & Magazines page.

An arrow's multipliers apply on top of whichever bow is firing it, so the words below describe the arrow rather than the finished shot.

Recovery is a sandbox option, so the percentages here are your current world's settings rather than the mod's defaults.

Every bow shot in this mod is permanently halved by the engine's two-handed grip test: the arrow displayed in your off hand means the game never sees the bow held in both hands. That is a deliberate, accepted trade for showing the nocked arrow at all.

The numbers below are the BOW's own contribution, before that halving and before the nocked arrow's own multiplier. See the Arrows page for the other half.

The practice target is built from the Carpentry menu under Furniture, and needs Woodwork 2.

Every aimed shot inside range hits it. There is no hit roll on the target itself, which makes it a pure practice tool rather than a test of your accuracy.

Arrows lodge in the target's face, up to twenty of them, and after that in its base. They are ordinary world items: walk up and pick them back up.

Shooting the target trains Archery at {TARGETXP} XP per hit, less than a zombie hit is worth.

The target has its own recovery sandbox option, separate from each arrow's. It is currently {TARGETRECOVERY}.

Drawing and holding a bow tires your arms. It is tracked as the same arm stiffness and Pain that every weapon uses, so it shows up in the usual moodles rather than anywhere special.

A compound bow's mechanical let-off makes it much cheaper to HOLD at full draw, even though drawing it in the first place costs what its number below implies. That is the whole point of a compound, and it is the let-off row rather than the strain row that tells the two apart.

Strain has no effect on your accuracy and none on your damage. What it costs you is comfort and time.

A bow remembers the last arrow you chose and picks it again on an empty reload. If you have run out of that one, it falls back to the best arrow you are carrying.

There are three ways to nock. Hold the reload key for the radial menu and choose an arrow; tap the reload key to nock the remembered or best arrow straight away; or right-click an arrow in your inventory and choose "Nock in (bow)". That same right-click menu also carries this handbook's own entry, so the two sit side by side.

The rack key - 'x' unless you have rebound it - un-nocks, and the arrow goes back into your inventory rather than being lost.

How long a nock takes depends on your Archery level and on the bow's draw weight. Each bow's nock speed is listed on the Bows page.

The Leather Quiver holds arrows and nothing else. It matches on the arrow tag rather than on a list of item IDs, so a sealed arrow pack cannot go in until you have opened it.

There is no cap on how many arrows fit - only the container's weight budget.

The bundle of arrows shown on a worn quiver is display only. It swaps between meshes at 1, 2, 3, 4, 5-6, 7-9 and 10 or more arrows, and carries no stat of its own.

Wearing a quiver speeds up every nock by {QUIVERBONUS}.

Every arrow that hits a zombie lodges something in it. Win the recovery roll and the whole arrow lodges; lose it and the arrow's Broken counterpart lodges instead. A lost roll never destroys the arrow outright.

Either way the arrow is visible, stuck in the zombie, and can be looted off the corpse.

Recovery chance is set per arrow and is a sandbox option, so a server can tune it. The Arrows page shows your own world's live value rather than the mod's default.

A Broken arrow is not waste. Right-click it and choose Repair: a window shows your chance, lets you pick which material to spend, and repairs one arrow or the whole stack. You need a crafting surface within reach, and a higher Fletching level makes each attempt succeed more often. See the Arrow crafting page.

Ten skill books ship: five for Archery and five for Fletching. Each one covers two levels, and reading it only speeds up how fast you gain XP - it never grants a level directly.

The two recipe magazines work differently. Reading The Nock & Fletch REPLACES every slow Fletching recipe with a faster version rather than adding a second entry beside it, and Skip the Shaft does the same for its four shortcut recipes. Your crafting list will not grow; the rows you already had simply get quicker.

The Archery Handbook is a reference, not a tutorial and not a quest log. Nothing here has to be read in order, and nothing on these pages tracks your progress.

Open it again at any time with {KEY}, or by right-clicking any RadArchery item in your inventory, which jumps straight to that item's page.

Every number shown throughout is read live from the mod's own data when the page is drawn, so a rebalance can never leave it stale.

The other eleven pages:
Archery skill - what the custom skill replaces, and how it is trained.
Nocking - the three ways to put an arrow on the string.
Recovery & Breakage - what becomes of an arrow after it hits.
Muscle strain - why holding a draw tires your arms.
Quiver - the Leather Quiver and its nock bonus.
Practice target - the buildable target and what it trains.
Bows - every bow, its stats and where it comes from.
Arrows - all ten arrows and their multipliers.
Arrowheads & Shafts - the crafting materials and the sealed packs.
Arrow crafting - the shape of the chain from wood to finished arrow.
Skill books & Magazines - the ten books and the two recipe magazines.
A repair was refused - nothing was spent.

Scales how much arm muscle strain drawing and holding a bow causes: a one-off cost when the draw starts, plus a drain for every second the aim is held. Heavier bows tire the arms faster, a compound bow's let-off makes it far easier to hold, and a higher Archery level tires them slower. Set to 0 to remove bow strain entirely. Applied on top of the game's own Muscle Strain Factor setting.

A straight wooden shaft cut and squared to length, bare and unfletched. Used to fletch arrows.
A fletched shaft tipped with a narrow forged bodkin point. Punches through cleanly and usually comes back intact. Fired from any bow.
A manufactured bullet point arrow on a carbon shaft. Slightly stronger than a Pinpoint carbon arrow. Fired from any bow.
A narrow, four-sided point forged to punch through rather than cut. Used to tip arrows.
A mass-produced bullet point, factory-sharp. Fits a Carbon Arrow Shaft.
A sealed case of 10 manufactured bullet points. Open it to get the heads out.
A sealed case of 5 manufactured bullet points. Open it to get the heads out.
A splinter of carcass bone worked to a sharp point. Used to tip arrows.
A fletched shaft with a sharpened bone point lashed to the end. Cuts as deep as flint, and is just as brittle. Fired from any bow.
A fletched shaft tipped with a wide forged broadhead. The hardest-hitting arrow you can craft, though it breaks more often. Fired from any bow.
A manufactured broadhead arrow on a carbon shaft. The hardest-hitting arrow in the mod. Fired from any bow.
A wide-bladed point forged and ground for a heavy wound. Used to tip arrows.
A mass-produced broadhead point, factory-ground. Fits a Carbon Arrow Shaft.
A sealed case of 10 manufactured broadhead points. Open it to get the heads out.
A sealed case of 5 manufactured broadhead points. Open it to get the heads out.
A snapped arrow, its shaft cracked and its fletching torn loose. Useless as ammunition. Can be re-fletched back into a working arrow.
A shipping crate of packed carbon hunting arrows. Open it to get the packs out.
A sealed retail pack of carbon hunting arrows. Open it to get the arrows out.
A manufactured carbon shaft, already fletched. Needs a point before it can be fired.
A sealed retail pack of carbon arrow shafts. Open it to get the shafts out.
A factory-made Pinpoint Carbon Arrow with a machined hunting point. Deadly and tough enough to shoot again and again, but it cannot be crafted -- only found. Fired from any bow.
A plain wooden shaft with a fire-hardened point and no fletching. Cheap to make, but weak, wayward and rarely worth recovering. Fired from any bow.
A wooden bow shaped and tillered with some care. Sturdier and stronger than a crude one. Draws and fires silently.
A limb of horn, carefully carved off an animal skull. Ready to be backed and bound into a bow.
A modern compound hunting bow. Its cams and cables put real power behind an arrow on an easy draw. Draws and fires silently.
A heavy-limbed compound hunting bow built for long shots. Hits hard and reaches far, but takes longer to draw. Draws and fires silently.
A bow hacked out of a green branch with a knife. Rough and weak, and it wears out quickly. Draws and fires silently.
A wooden bow stave faced with fiberglass tape and bonded with epoxy. Needs stringing to become a bow.
A wooden shaft fletched with three vanes and whittled to a point. Flies far truer than a bare shaft, though it still hits lightly. Fired from any bow.
A carefully carved wooden bow, tillered even and bound with leather. Strong and hard-wearing. Draws and fires silently.
An arrow shaft bound with three fletchings and a length of cord, still without a point. Sharpen it or fit an arrowhead to finish the arrow.
A handful of vanes cut from feathers, stiff card or bottle plastic. Used to fletch arrows.
A wood-cored bow backed with sinew and horn carved from a skull, wrapped in leather. The strongest bow a survivor can build without a factory.
A stitched leather quiver worn on the hip. Holds arrows and nothing else, keeping them to hand and out of your pack.
A scrap of thin metal cut and shaped into a point. Used to tip arrows.
A modern recurve bow, its wood core faced with fiberglass tape and bonded with epoxy. Hits harder than anything carved by hand.
A piece of flint knapped down to a sharp point and edge. Used to tip arrows.
A fletched shaft with a knapped flint point lashed to the end. Cuts deep, but stone is brittle and often chips on impact. Fired from any bow.
A fletched shaft with a scrap-metal head bound to the end. Hits a little softer than stone or bone, but survives the shot more often. Fired from any bow.
A straw-stuffed practice target on a wooden frame. Shoot it to train Archery, then pull your arrows back out of it.
